lane.name: New alt-country and honky-tonk bands
lane.definition: 2010s–2020s bands and songwriters playing recognizable country (honky-tonk, '90s country, bluegrass-inflected) with indie-scene provenance, labels, and audiences.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: Meek's solo debut, looser and more overtly country than Big Thief. It is built on plain, warm Telecaster twang and easygoing melodies, with his reedy voice sitting relaxed in front of the band.
albums.lineage: Establishes Meek's separate honky-tonk-adjacent solo identity outside Big Thief, rooted in his Texas upbringing.

albums.label: Rounder Records
albums.description: Ruston Kelly's debut is the sound he calls 'dirt emo': confessional, downcast lyrics about addiction and heartbreak set over pedal steel and plainspoken country-rock arrangements, closer in mood to emo than to Music Row polish. It moves between hushed acoustic laments and fuller, rootsy full-band tracks without losing its diary-like intimacy. It is a gateway record for listeners coming to alt-country from indie/emo rather than from classic country.
albums.lineage: Draws on Nashville's neo-traditional and outlaw country vocabulary but bends it toward emo's confessional mode, a hybrid Kelly himself named 'dirt emo' and one that seems to echo across later indie-adjacent country songwriting.

albums.label: New West Records
albums.description: A full-band collaboration with New Zealand's Marlon Williams, Plastic Bouquet brightens Kacy & Clayton's usual spare Canadian prairie folk into warmer, harmony-heavy country rock. Williams and Kacy Anderson's voices trade and blend across a set of plainspoken duets.
albums.lineage: A one-off widening of Kacy & Clayton's traditional-leaning catalog through collaboration with Marlon Williams, closer to breezy country rock than their usual austere folk.

albums.label: Verve Forecast Records
albums.description: Kentucky songwriter S.G. Goodman's debut is a rocking, rootsy country-folk record steeped in her rural western-Kentucky upbringing, produced by My Morning Jacket's Jim James. Her keening voice and reverb-heavy guitars make it a stark, plainspoken start to her catalog.
albums.lineage: Sounds close to Tyler Childers and Ian Noe in the Kentucky storyteller wing of the new country scene.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: Katie Crutchfield's fifth Waxahatchee album traded her indie-rock guitars for a warmer, twangier palette of pedal steel and loping tempos, written in the wake of getting sober. The plainspoken lyrics about family, memory and the South made it one of the most acclaimed records of 2020. It is often cited as a turning point for indie musicians leaning into country.
albums.lineage: Grows out of Crutchfield's earlier lo-fi indie-rock work into full country songwriting, leading directly to the Plains project with Jess Williamson and sitting at the front of a wider wave of indie musicians leaning into twang.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: A warmer, more full-band record than his debut, with ramshackle, patient country-rock songs and groove-locked guitar interplay.
albums.lineage: Deepens Meek's alt-country songwriting voice ahead of his move to 4AD for Haunted Mountain.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Aaron Dowdy's self-released full-length debut as Fust is a lo-fi, plainspoken alt-country record, its narrators drifting through small Southern towns and bad decisions. It set the template the band expanded on with a full lineup on Genevieve and Big Ugly. A quieter, more private-sounding entry point into the band's catalog.
albums.lineage: Fust's founding document, before the fuller alt-country sound the band pursued once signed to Dear Life Records.

albums.label: Propeller Sound Recordings
albums.description: Chapel Hill songwriter and literature professor Florence Dore blends classic-rock hooks, Americana twang and 1980s college-radio jangle. Narrative-heavy lyrics and a lived-in, veteran band sound keep it far from Nashville polish. It is built for listeners who want literate, well-crafted country-rock steeped in the history of the genre's indie wing.
albums.lineage: Sounds steeped in the 1980s-'90s college-rock and No Depression alt-country lineage that C3 grew from.

albums.album: I Walked with You a Ways
albums.label: Anti-
albums.description: A duo album pairing Katie Crutchfield (Waxahatchee) with fellow songwriter Jess Williamson, built around plush '90s-country vocal harmonies and pedal steel over breakup-and-friendship songs. It plays like a loving homage to Lucinda Williams and Trisha Yearwood-style country radio filtered through two indie songwriters. A key document of the indie scene's 2020s country turn.
albums.lineage: A direct collaborative offshoot of Waxahatchee's country pivot, pairing Crutchfield with Jess Williamson's own move from folk toward country songwriting.

albums.label: Verve Forecast Records
albums.description: Goodman's second album sharpens her rural-Kentucky storytelling into a bleaker, more electric record about depression and rural isolation. The arrangements lean harder into fuzzy guitar than her debut without losing its plainspoken drawl. A more confident, harder-hitting follow-up.
albums.lineage: Extends Old Time Feeling's western-Kentucky storytelling into darker territory; sounds close to Ian Noe and the post-Childers Kentucky scene.
key_tracks: All My Love Is Coming Back to Me

albums.label: Rounder Records
albums.description: Calgary-born, bluegrass-trained singer Bella White's second album pairs striking opening lines about moving on with Appalachian-rooted picking. It widens her sound with country, indie and classic-rock textures without losing the traditional bluegrass core.
albums.lineage: Sounds like the Appalachian bluegrass tradition seen through a young Canadian songwriter's lens.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Blue County Pistol's EP is a rollicking, banjo-heavy alt-country release, warm and instantly familiar in its melodies. It plays like a tight, focused introduction rather than a sprawling statement.
albums.lineage: Part of the wider Bandcamp-driven alt-country underground, sharing the banjo-and-drawl approach of countless small self-released country EPs of the early 2020s.

albums.label: 4AD
albums.description: Meek's 4AD debut, patient, ramshackle folk-rock songs built on groove-locked guitar work, sung in his easy, unhurried drawl.
albums.lineage: Meek's first release for 4AD, the label Big Thief also records for, bringing his alt-country solo work to a wider audience.

albums.label: Dear Life Records
albums.description: Fust's Dear Life Records debut fills out Aaron Dowdy's plainspoken songwriting with a full band. The songs mix wry, character-driven storytelling with a loose, unhurried alt-country backing of pedal steel and piano.
albums.lineage: Expands Evil Joy's lo-fi songwriting into a fuller band sound after signing to Dear Life Records, setting up Big Ugly.

albums.label: Yep Roc
albums.description: Jobi Riccio's debut is coming-of-age country songwriting built on pedal steel, fiddle, and small full-band arrangements, moving from tender acoustic ballads to fuller alt-country arrangements without losing its intimate, diaristic voice. Songs about self-love, loneliness, and growing up in your twenties are sung plainly, without Nashville gloss. It suits listeners who want 2020s indie-scene country that still plays like a singer-songwriter record.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with 2020s indie-Americana peers who bring 2010s indie-folk intimacy into recognizably country arrangements.

albums.label: Scissor Tail Records
albums.description: The Chicago band's debut mixes cosmic country and psychedelic choogle with straight honky-tonk, split between co-lead singers Chris Coleslaw and Lexi Goddard. Pedal steel and reverb-soaked guitars sit under barroom, heartbreak-and-hangover songwriting. It is an unpolished debut that established the band's neon-lit, small-hours sound.
albums.lineage: Draws on classic honky-tonk duet singing and cosmic country in the Gram Parsons/Emmylou Harris mold, feeding directly into the band's more widely reviewed follow-up Horses.

albums.label: Nameless Knight Records
albums.description: John Prine's son makes an unhurried, plainspoken singer-songwriter record about grief and inheritance, built on fingerpicked acoustic guitar and a warm, understated voice that avoids leaning on his father's shadow. Songs like the title track work through loss directly rather than cleverly, closer to quiet country-folk than to barroom wit. It gives the C3 scene a straight-line link back to the '70s country-folk storytellers by blood as well as sound.
albums.lineage: The most literal lineage in the atlas: son of John Prine, carrying the plainspoken country-folk storytelling tradition (V25) directly into the 2020s indie-country scene.

albums.album: JP Harris Is a Trash Fire
albums.label: Bloodshot Records
albums.description: Nashville honky-tonker JP Harris makes self-aware, satirical country songwriting here, gutting and funny often in the same verse. Fiddle, steel and a tight honky-tonk band back a pointed, personal voice.
albums.lineage: Follows Harris's years fronting JP Harris and the Tough Choices, landing him on Bloodshot's insurgent-country roster.

albums.label: Lightning Rod Records
albums.description: Jesse Daniel plays it straight: shuffling honky-tonk rhythms, crying pedal steel and a plain, traditionalist voice on songs about recovery, the road and old-school country. Coming out of California punk rather than a Nashville pipeline, Daniel's traditionalism is a chosen, DIY revival rather than an inherited style. It is a straightforward entry point for listeners who want honky-tonk played by someone raised on punk rock.
albums.lineage: A cowpunk-to-honky-tonk arc in miniature: Daniel's background in California punk bands leads into a self-consciously traditionalist sound that recalls Bakersfield, released through the independent, Nashville-based Lightning Rod Records.

albums.label: Thirty Tigers / Miss Freedomland
albums.description: Halfsies is Lizzie No's modern Americana record, carried by a genre-fluid songwriting voice and her harp alongside twangy band arrangements. It balances pedal-steel warmth with sharp, personal storytelling. It suits listeners who like country with a wry, independent streak.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to the wider Black country and cosmic-country revival within the neighboring C3 scene.

albums.label: Anti-
albums.description: Waxahatchee's sixth album deepens the country turn of Saint Cloud with a full touring-band feel, guitar and harmonies from MJ Lenderman, and some of Crutchfield's most direct, hook-driven songwriting. It is a good entry point for the wider indie-to-country scene of the mid-2020s.
albums.lineage: A continuation of the country-facing sound Crutchfield established on Saint Cloud, cementing the connection between the Waxahatchee/Plains circle and the Asheville MJ Lenderman scene.

albums.label: Merge Records
albums.description: Case Oats' debut album, led by singer Casey Gomez Walker, is an assured set of character studies backed by pedal steel and fiddle. It moves easily between confessional-poem weight and conversational ease. A confident debut from a young Chicago band.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with Chicago's indie-country circle and the wider Waxahatchee/MJ Lenderman scene.

albums.label: Dear Life Records
albums.description: Fust's third album is a detail-rich, character-driven record about visiting a grandmother's childhood Appalachian neighborhood, cut with help from Alex Farrar and members of Sluice. It is the band's fullest and most widely heard record to date.
albums.lineage: Continues Fust's Dear Life Records run, cementing the North Carolina country-textured songwriting line that runs alongside Wednesday and MJ Lenderman's Asheville-adjacent scene.

albums.label: Sophomore Lounge
albums.description: Kentucky songwriter Grace Rogers' debut LP puts conversational, character-based storytelling over jangly electric guitar and a friendly, unpolished full-band sound. Her lyrics have a poet's eye for small-town and family detail. A warm, inviting entry point into the Louisville indie-country scene around Sophomore Lounge.
albums.lineage: A Sophomore Lounge release from the same Louisville scene as Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band; sounds rooted in old-time and string-band music.

albums.label: New West Records
albums.description: Hedley's third album keeps building on his throwback Nashville-Sound sound with New West, continuing the honky-tonk revivalism of Neon Blue. It is the most recent entry in a catalog built entirely around classic-country authenticity rather than novelty. A steady, dependable extension of his sound.
albums.lineage: Extends Hedley's classic-country throwback catalog for a third record on New West Records.

albums.label: Rounder Records
albums.description: Tulsa songwriter Ken Pomeroy's stripped-back, autobiographical collection of contemporary folk-country, drawing on her Cherokee heritage and coming-of-age stories. It is a brutally honest, unshowy record built around voice, guitar and close harmonies.
albums.lineage: Sits alongside the Oklahoma/Texas red-dirt songwriter tradition, sharing an audience with the Sturgill Simpson/outlaw-adjacent wing of the new country scene.

albums.label: Slough Water Records
albums.description: Goodman's third album turns toward the folk-magic and planting traditions of rural Kentucky for its imagery. It keeps the plainspoken, rootsy sound of her earlier records while widening its spiritual and agricultural language. A settled, personal record from one of the scene's most distinctive Kentucky voices.
albums.lineage: Continues Goodman's western-Kentucky storytelling; its imagery draws on the region's folk traditions.

albums.label: Scissor Tail Records
albums.description: Tobacco City's second album widens their neon-lit country sound with more players and fuller arrangements while keeping the boozy small-town nostalgia of their debut. It channels '70s country touchstones like Gram Parsons, with duet vocals and pedal steel. A confident, more fully arranged follow-up to Tobacco City, USA.
albums.lineage: A direct sequel to Tobacco City, USA; sounds indebted to Gram Parsons-style cosmic country.

albums.label: Anti-
albums.description: Nashville songwriter Brennan Wedl's self-titled debut full-length blends arena-scaled country-rock hooks with swaggering, confessional lyrics. It moves between honky-tonk pastiche ('Fake Cowboy') and glammy indie rock without losing its country backbone.
albums.lineage: An Anti- release that sounds close to the Waxahatchee/Snocaps country-rock circle.

albums.label: 4AD
albums.description: Meek's latest solo album, built around his wiry guitar lines and reedy, gentle voice as he digs into questions of love and self-reflection. It is for listeners who like their alt-country relaxed and a little off-center.
albums.lineage: Continues Meek's alt-country solo catalog after his earlier records.

albums.label: New West Records
albums.description: Nenni widens her honky-tonk base with soul horns and organ while keeping her focus on the dancefloor as a place of escape and self-acceptance. The songwriting turns more explicitly toward self-forgiveness and imperfection, sung in her bright, twangy voice.
albums.lineage: Extends Nenni's honky-tonk catalog toward Southern soul, a crossover that sounds close to Margo Price's and Jaime Wyatt's later albums.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Kiely Connell's debut record is sparse, unburdened alt-country songwriting. The arrangements stay spare and intimate, built to foreground her plainspoken, unsettled lyrics. A quietly confident debut steeped in Midwestern small-town detail.
albums.lineage: Sounds like a Midwestern-to-Nashville songwriter story typical of the current alt-country scene.

albums.label: Ever/Never Records
albums.description: Chicago's National Photo Committee plays raucous, country-tinged bar rock, with spidery pedal steel lines cutting through gravelly, shouted vocals. Its songs favor an unresisting, rowdy energy over polish, closer to a loud honky-tonk stage than a studio. A record built to be heard live.
albums.lineage: Part of the same Chicago DIY-country circle as Tobacco City and Red PK, connecting the city's cowpunk-adjacent bar-rock scene to the wider Bandcamp alt-country revival.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A Chicago songwriter's hushed, banjo-and-pedal-steel folk-country. The songs are intimate and unshowy, closer to a bedroom recording than a full-band statement.
albums.lineage: Sounds close to the Chicago cosmic-country scene around Tobacco City.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Chicago-by-way-of-Minnesota songwriter Tommy Goodroad's debut studio album mixes Midwestern folksy roots music with rollicking classic honky-tonk, co-produced by Amos Pitsch (Tenement, Hotline TNT). Backed by his touring band the Highway Birds, it leans on fiddle and pedal steel over a rowdy country-rock backbone. A confident full-band debut after years of live shows.
albums.lineage: Part of the same Chicago DIY-country network as Case Oats and Tobacco City, blending Midwestern roots music with classic honky-tonk and outlaw touches.
